title: Vous êtes toute ma famille  (You're All My Family)

segments.t: She opened her bank's website and stared at her account. Then, to take her mind off it, she tried a dating site, and a chat with a stranger went badly wrong; she logged off, furious. Now, exhausted, she joins Arlette, the oldest agent in Paris, and her little dog Jean Gabin. As usual, French first, and don't worry about every word.
Ça va, chérie? Tu es en retard.
Un café?
Oui, merci, Damien.
J'ai mal dormi.
Tu as fait la fête?
Ouais, c'était dingue!
J'ai passé la nuit sur le site de ma banque.
Et toi?
Moi aussi, j'ai fait mes comptes.
Autant dépenser ce que j'ai pour l'agence.
Ton assurance-vie? Tu es sûre?
Je n'ai pas d'enfants, à part Jean Gabin.
Alors, à quoi bon?
Vous êtes toute ma famille. Vous tous et mes acteurs.
Merci, Arlette.
Tu veux faire pipi, Jean Gabin?
Attendez, il fait pipi!
Let's go through it. Arlette greets Andréa with a word of affection and a little telling-off.
Ça va, chérie? Tu es en retard.
'All right, darling? You're late.' The word for 'darling' is feminine here, because she's talking to a woman. And Arlette uses the casual 'you' with her younger colleague.
Un café?
'A coffee?' Damien, the waiter, knows them well.
Oui, merci, Damien.
'Yes, thanks, Damien.' Simple and friendly.
J'ai mal dormi.
'I slept badly.' The everyday past tense: the verb 'have', then the action. The word for 'badly' sits in the middle.
Tu as fait la fête?
'Were you out partying?' Literally 'did you make the party?'. That's the French way to say you went out and had fun.
Ouais, c'était dingue!
'Yeah, it was wild!' The first word is the casual 'yes', and the last is a slangy word for 'crazy'. She's being ironic, of course.
J'ai passé la nuit sur le site de ma banque.
'I spent the night on my bank's website.' In French it's 'the site of my bank': the owner comes last.
Et toi?
'And you?' The strong form of the casual 'you', used after 'and'.
Moi aussi, j'ai fait mes comptes.
'Me too, I did my accounts.' Arlette has been counting her money as well.
Autant dépenser ce que j'ai pour l'agence.
'I might as well spend what I have on the agency.' The first word gives the idea 'might as well'. Arlette has made up her mind.
Ton assurance-vie? Tu es sûre?
'Your life insurance? Are you sure?' The word for 'sure' takes an extra letter, because Arlette is a woman.
Je n'ai pas d'enfants, à part Jean Gabin.
'I have no children, apart from Jean Gabin.' After a negative, the word for 'some' shrinks to a tiny linking word before the noun. And Jean Gabin, named after a famous French actor, is her dog.
Alors, à quoi bon?
'So, what's the point?' Arlette uses a short, fixed expression that literally means 'to what good?'.
Vous êtes toute ma famille.
'You're all my family.' Here the formal 'you' is really the plural one: she means all of them at the agency.
Vous tous et mes acteurs.
'All of you, and my actors.' The agency is her whole life.
Merci, Arlette.
'Thank you, Arlette.' Andréa is touched.
Tu veux faire pipi, Jean Gabin?
'Do you need to pee, Jean Gabin?' Literally 'do you want to do pee-pee?', the way you'd talk to a child, or a dog.
Attendez, il fait pipi!

'Wait, he's peeing!' Too late. The waiter's command uses the formal 'you', the polite form a waiter uses with customers. So the tender moment ends with a puddle on the terrace. Now the whole breakfast once more, in French.
Ça va, chérie? Tu es en retard.
Un café?
Oui, merci, Damien.
J'ai mal dormi.
Tu as fait la fête?
Ouais, c'était dingue!
J'ai passé la nuit sur le site de ma banque.
Et toi?
Moi aussi, j'ai fait mes comptes.
Autant dépenser ce que j'ai pour l'agence.
Ton assurance-vie? Tu es sûre?
Je n'ai pas d'enfants, à part Jean Gabin.
Alors, à quoi bon?
Vous êtes toute ma famille. Vous tous et mes acteurs.
Merci, Arlette.
Tu veux faire pipi, Jean Gabin?
Attendez, il fait pipi!
That's the end of this scene: a sad night, then a warm morning, all in French. When you watch it, listen for Arlette telling them they're all her family. See you next time!
À tout à l'heure!
